title: Generate–Verify–Repair for Intent‑Driven Network Changes: Controlled Evaluation with a Deterministic Verifier
abstract: We evaluate whether a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline—single‑shot LLM generation followed by a deterministic network verifier and up to one automated repair—reduces accepted unsafe network changes versus LLM‑only generation on a standardized synthetic NetOps intent workload. In a preregistered paired design (study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29) we ran N=500 distinct synthetic intents (shared single initial candidate per intent) with generation by gpt-5-mini and adjudication by a deterministic verifier. Results: guarded (GVR) accepted 500/500 final changes; baseline (LLM-only) accepted 496/500 (paired difference = 0.008). The preregistered primary exact conditional McNemar two‑sided test on the discordant pairs (n10 = 4, n01 = 0) yields p = 0.125 computed as 2 * PBinom(X ≥ 4; n = 4, p = 0.5). An exploratory paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.002, 0.016] (bootstrap predeclared exploratory and interpreted cautiously given only four discordants). Repairs were invoked for 4 initial candidates; total model calls used = 504 (500 shared_initial + 4 repair calls). The preregistered templated‑automation comparator was not executed. Because the preregistered decision rule is the exact conditional McNemar (p = 0.125), we do not claim confirmatory statistical significance. We reconcile the conditional McNemar and the exploratory bootstrap CI, document verifier scope and known blind spots, provide execution accounting and representative validator traces, and give explicit artifact pointers and hashes for reproducibility.

sections.introduction: Translating operator intent into device configuration is a promising NetOps automation vector but remains risky: syntactic mistakes, incorrect sequencing, or transient availability violations can cause outages. Large language models (LLMs) can produce human‑readable CLI sequences from intent descriptions, yet hallucination and factual errors threaten operational safety. A practical, immediately actionable mitigation is a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline: (1) produce a candidate configuration with an LLM; (2) deterministically verify the candidate against encoded workflow and policy rules; (3) if verification fails, issue a bounded automated repair attempt and re‑verify. This work tests whether a bounded GVR pipeline (single initial generation + deterministic verification + at most one repair) reduces the rate of accepted verifier‑failing changes relative to LLM‑only generation on a controlled synthetic NetOps workload. We executed a preregistered paired trial (study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29) comparing GVR to baseline LLM acceptance across N = 500 intents, with artifacts and analysis archived for reproducibility. Our contributions are (1) a preregistered paired trial executed end‑to‑end with archived artifacts; (2) an evidence‑grounded description of generation, deterministic verifier semantics, and a bounded automated repair policy; (3) reconciled inferential presentation (pre‑specified exact conditional McNemar plus exploratory paired bootstrap CI) with explicit contingency counts and p‑value computation; and (4) execution accounting, representative validator traces, and a limitations discussion that links verifier semantics to operational external validity.
sections.related_work: Three literatures motivate this experiment. Survey and systems research document growing use of LLMs for intent‑driven configuration, AIOps, and multi‑agent NetOps orchestration while highlighting hallucination and correctness as deployment obstacles. Methodological work on tool‑augmented LLMs and generate–validate–repair architectures proposes deterministic verifiers or simulators to raise operational assurance and calls for standardized evaluation practices. Deterministic configuration verifiers and scalable analyzers (Batfish‑style tools and distributed verifiers) provide feasible oracles for many syntactic and workflow properties, but prior empirical work rarely combines preregistration, paired designs, and full archival artifacts at this scale. Our study situates itself at the intersection: a controlled paired trial that uses a deterministic verifier as the operational adjudicator and an explicitly bounded automated repair loop. Key verified references that shaped scope and design include surveys and system papers on LLMs for NetOps and tool‑augmented agents (cited_record_ids), methodological blueprints for verifier‑guided generation, and verifier‑system publications documenting practical verifier semantics and scaling considerations.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and primary estimand: The experiment was preregistered as study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29. The primary estimand is the paired success‑rate difference (GVR − baseline) across N = 500 distinct intents stratified across 10 synthetic topology profiles (50 intents per profile). Sampling seeds, the deterministic task generator, and the analysis executor were frozen before execution (preregistration SHA‑256 = aa8982a27c73e51521ac023a78adcfa358ef3978c0f9bc05213801fcbd2f1d0a). The preregistered confirmatory test is the two‑sided exact conditional McNemar test computed on discordant pairs; a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729) was pre‑specified as exploratory.
Generation and orchestration: For each intent a single shared_initial_generation candidate was produced by the declared model gpt-5-mini (declared_model_version recorded in execution/model_configuration.json; model_configuration.json SHA‑256 = a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820). The GVR controller validated the shared candidate with the deterministic verifier deterministic_netops_validator_v5. If verification failed, the controller invoked at most one automated repair attempt (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). The baseline condition accepts the shared candidate without verifier‑driven repair. Provider‑call accounting (execution manifest) reports hosted_model_call_event_count = 504 and stage_counts mapping shared_initial_generation = 500 and repair = 4.
Deterministic verifier semantics and codebook: The primary verifier executes a canonical pipeline on normalized CLI sequences: (i) syntactic parsing and normalization; (ii) workflow and required‑sequence checks (e.g., must_be_down_for_fields, all_down_before_any_field_change); (iii) availability/group constraints (exactly_active, minimum_active_in_groups); (iv) dependency and paired‑field enforcement (paired MTU changes, equal_final_fields); and (v) final‑state comparison against the task expected_final_state. The verifier emits normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation list with violation codes, and a boolean valid flag per episode. A nonempty violation set yields a failing outcome. The human‑readable verifier codebook (violation‑code → short description) is archived in the execution artifacts; its manifest entry (path and SHA‑256) is recorded in the full execution manifest (execution/execution_manifest.json) within the evidence bundle for direct retrieval. Representative verifier_trace JSON objects are archived under execution/scoring/ and include validation_before/validation_after diagnostics and the validator_version = 5.0 marker.
Repair template and acceptance: When the verifier fails a shared_initial candidate, the GVR controller issues at most one repair prompt to the same generation model using a constrained repair template containing the original intent abstraction plus the verifier violation codes and short descriptions. A repair candidate is accepted only if the verifier returns valid=true. Repair invocations and acceptance outcomes are logged in execution/scoring/ and in provider traces; four repair calls occurred in the archived run.
Statistical procedures and preregistered handling of missingness: Primary confirmatory inference used the two‑sided exact conditional McNemar test implemented as the conditional binomial on discordant pairs: given discordant totals n = n10 + n01 and k = n10, the two‑sided p‑value equals p = 2 * sum_{x=k}^{n} Binom(n,x) * 0.5^{n}. We report the exact conditional computation with the observed contingency inputs (n10 = 4, n01 = 0). The exploratory paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI resamples paired outcomes (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) and recomputes the paired difference per resample. Primary missingness handling used complete pairs (complete_pair_count = 500); the run recorded zero failed episodes so no pairwise imputation was required.
sections.results:
Execution summary and primary counts: The run completed completed_episode_count = 1000 (500 intents × 2 conditions) with model_calls_used = 504. The condition summary (analysis/condition_summary.csv; archived) reports baseline successes 496/500 (0.992) and guarded successes 500/500 (1.000). The paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is n11 = 496, n10 = 4, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Repairs were invoked for the four initial candidates corresponding to the four discordant pairs (n10 = 4); all four repair attempts produced verifier‑passing candidates. Mean model calls per accepted change ≈ 504/500 = 1.008, quantifying the bounded repair policy's low incremental model cost for this workload.
Confirmatory exact McNemar computation: Observed discordant total n = n10 + n01 = 4 with k = n10 = 4. Under the preregistered conditional McNemar two‑sided formulation the p‑value is p = 2 * PBinom(X ≥ 4; n = 4, p = 0.5). For n = 4, PBinom(X ≥ 4; n = 4, p = 0.5) = (1/16), so p = 2 * (1/16) = 0.125. Because this exact conditional test was the preregistered decision rule, we do not claim confirmatory statistical significance for the primary estimand.
Exploratory paired bootstrap interval and reconciliation: The preregistered exploratory paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) for the paired difference is [0.002, 0.016] (analysis artifacts: analysis/paired_difference_figure.svg and analysis/analysis_log.jsonl). The bootstrap was predeclared exploratory and differs from the conditional McNemar in conditioning: McNemar conditions on observed margins (fixes row/column totals) and evaluates the exact binomial tail of discordant outcomes; bootstrap resampling of paired outcomes does not condition on the observed margins and therefore can yield a CI that excludes zero even when the conditional McNemar is non‑significant. With small discordant counts (n = 4) bootstrap percentile intervals have poor frequentist coverage and should be interpreted cautiously; we therefore present both perspectives and follow the preregistered decision rule for confirmatory claims.
Representative repaired example (artifact‑grounded): Representative task manifest and response artifacts are archived. Example (artifact pointers): pair_id = pair-000004 (task_id = task-000004). The archived shared_initial response (execution/responses/task-000004-shared-initial.txt; SHA‑256 = 2d39d60da792238fd01ca432228fcec6a2fcc4449be99532c66e8a907a39ccd8) contains the initial generated CLI sequence. The task_manifest entry (execution/task_manifest.jsonl; SHA‑256 = 5a822e787302a0b3bb03a86a81b20564a44e2636731f853f9d45ac12e4876cc8) records the required_sequence and the intent abstraction. The scoring JSON (execution/scoring/task-000004-baseline.json) archives the verifier_trace entries showing the violation codes emitted and the subsequent repair application recorded in the guarded condition; these artifacts exemplify how the verifier codebook guided a single constrained repair that resulted in a verifier pass. The four repaired episodes share similar violation patterns (sequence or availability errors) that the repair prompt corrected under the bounded repair policy.
Cost accounting and provider audit: The deterministic_reconciliation artifact records provider_call_audit details including hosted_model_call_event_count = 504, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 504, failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 0, cache_hit_count = 0, cache_miss_count = 504, and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 500, repair: 4}. These counts quantify model call overhead and show that observed repair frequency was very low for this synthetic workload.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation: The GVR pipeline intercepted four verifier‑detectable unsafe initial candidates that baseline would have accepted, at modest model overhead. Under the preregistered conditional exact McNemar (p = 0.125) the effect is not confirmatory. The exploratory bootstrap CI excludes zero but should be read as descriptive: bootstrap resampling does not condition on observed margins and with only four discordants can produce intervals with poor frequentist properties. Because the exact conditional McNemar was preregistered as the decision rule, we do not assert confirmatory significance.
Verifier coverage and blind spots: The deterministic verifier enforces canonical normalization, required sequencing, availability/group constraints, dependency and paired‑field rules, and final‑state equality to the task expected_final_state. Passing this verifier is necessary for the experiment’s definition of safety but is not sufficient for all real‑world hazards: the verifier does not model vendor‑specific CLI semantics, control‑plane convergence timing, hardware resource exhaustion, or out‑of‑band side effects. The human‑readable verifier codebook (violation‑code → description) is archived and its manifest entry (path and SHA‑256) is recorded in the execution manifest for retrieval; consult the archived execution/execution_manifest.json to locate the codebook artifact entry.
Operational implications and cost tradeoffs: Deterministic verification plus a bounded repair loop can remove verifier‑detectable unsafe outputs with low overhead for workloads with low initial failure rates. The observed low repair rate (4/500) produced mean model calls per accepted change ≈ 1.008; workloads with higher initial hallucination or adversarial inputs will raise repair frequency, increasing model‑call cost and possibly verifier load. Real production adoption requires scaling verifier fidelity (vendor parsers, control‑plane simulators), quantifying verifier runtime and resource costs, and multi‑model replication to test robustness against generator variation.
Threats to validity: Internal validity is strong (preregistration, fixed seeds, complete pairs). Construct validity is limited by verifier abstractions and synthetic device templates (synthetic_topologies_v1, synthetic_device_configs_v1). External validity is constrained by single‑model scope (gpt-5-mini) and synthetic topologies; multi‑model replication and vendor‑specific CLI tests are needed to generalize. Conclusion validity was affected by realized margins: the preregistered power plan targeted an effect ≈ 0.08, but the observed near‑ceiling baseline (0.992) produced only four discordants, reducing realized power relative to the preregistered assumption. The preregistered templated‑automation comparator was not executed, so the original two‑test Bonferroni familywise plan could not be fully applied.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired trial (N = 500) using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic verifier, a generate–verify–repair pipeline repaired four verifier‑detectable unsafe initial candidates at modest model‑call cost (4 repairs; model_calls_used = 504). The paired difference = 0.008 yields an exploratory bootstrap 95% CI [0.002, 0.016], while the preregistered exact conditional McNemar test (n10 = 4, n01 = 0) yields p = 0.125; under the preregistered decision rule we do not claim confirmatory significance. Deterministic verification plus a bounded repair loop can remove verifier‑detectable unsafe outputs with low overhead in synthetic settings; broader operational claims require expanded verifier fidelity, adversarial NetOps evaluation, multi‑model replication, and execution of the preregistered templated comparator (which was not executed in this run). All primary execution and analysis artifacts cited here are archived in the evidence bundle for independent verification; key artifact hashes and pointers are listed in the Disclosure Statement and in the execution manifest entries referenced above.

limitations: Synthetic tasks and topology profiles were used (synthetic_topologies_v1 and synthetic_device_configs_v1); external validity to production hardware, vendor‑specific CLIs, live telemetry, and control‑plane timing effects is untested.
Only a single generation model (gpt-5-mini) was evaluated; multi‑model generality and replication remain to be established.

Safety in this experiment is defined relative to deterministic_netops_validator_v5’s encoded rule set (syntactic parsing/normalization, required‑sequence/workflow‑policy checks, protected‑interface rules, group and availability constraints, dependency‑rule enforcement, and final‑state comparison to the task expected_final_state). Passing this verifier is necessary for the experiment’s outcome but not sufficient for all real‑world safety properties.

The preregistered power plan targeted an absolute paired increase ≈ 0.08 (8 percentage points). The observed baseline success rate (496/500 = 0.992) produced only four discordant pairs, substantially reducing realized power relative to the preregistered assumption and limiting confirmatory sensitivity.

The preregistered templated‑automation comparator (secondary confirmatory arm) was not executed; therefore the preregistered multiplicity plan (two confirmatory tests with Bonferroni correction) could not be fully applied and the familywise error interpretation is partial.
